newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan rights group says violations increasing.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan rights group says violations increasing.

text.p: A Kenyan human rights group on Wednesday blamed the government for failing to halt extra-judicial killings, torture, restrictions on movements and theft of public land.

"In the last six months KHRC has been receiving horrifying accounts of torture in custody. Regular police shoot 'suspects' in the streets, administrative police systematically torture their suspects to death in custody," the Kenya Human Rights Commission (KHRC) said.

"The government has a primary responsibility to protect and enhance human rights but has shown no commitment to this. The government has not come out with a clear and unequivocal policy denouncing violence," it said.
KHRC spokesman Njuguna Mutahi said the group was investigating allegations that police tortured seven poeple accused of robbery in central Kenya.
Reporters said some of seven suspects, including three former soldiers, had gaping wounds when they appeared in court in Nyahururu, 200 km (125 miles) north of Nairobi, on Tuesday.
They said one suspect was unconscious in a police cell in handcuffs while another lay prostrate in court in pain.
A magistrate has asked police to explain the assault.
"While the commission supports the police on the need to tackle crime, the force must show accountability when the right to life has been violated," the report for January to June said.
"The current state where the police are judges and executioners leaves a lot of room for criminal elements in the force to take advantage," the report added.

In the report, the commission said there had been a marked increase of human rights violations, especially extra-judicial killings, torture, restrictions on freedom of movement and association, unlawful demolitions and theft of public land.
A spokesman at Attorney-General Amos Wako's office said Wako had not seen the report and had therefore no immediate comment.
A police spokesman was also not available to comment.
The report added that the chief of police and attorney-general were not keen on prosecuting police officers or taking other action against officers indicted by the testimony of witnesses.
Though no executions have taken place in Kenya since 1985, the commission noted that 55 people were sentenced to death between January and June, an average of about 10 per month.

"The death sentence is barbaric, inhuman, abhorrent and punitive. It has not proved its worth as deterrent to crime. There is also a danger of it being used as a political weapon against government critics...," it said.
The commission reported ethnic violence in Kenya's northern region, where 35 people were killed between June 19 and last month in what police described as cattle rustling.

"Fatal clashes cannot be dismissed as cattle rustling," the report said. "The government's failure to admit the reality of the violence proves that cattle rustling has been used as a cover-up for ethnic violence in this country."
